mappings.note: 'Political emancipation' is lifted straight from the speech; a retrieval MCQ, LO-1.
Why love is easier to learn than hate is Mandela's claim about human nature - the writer's message, LO-2.
Apartheid as the cause of the lasting wound is stated outright; retrieval, LO-1.
Asks for the significance of 'we, who were outlaws' against the political system that came before - reading the line in its historical context, LO-2.
The shared loss of humanity for oppressor and oppressed is Mandela's argument, so the writer's message (LO-2) rather than a retrievable pair of facts.
Extract item: the lead part asks for an inference about Mandela and what he intends by 'God bless Africa' (LO-2); the remaining parts work from the pledge stated in the extract (LO-1).
Two of the three parts turn on expressions - 'rainbow gathering' and a substitute for 'pleasantly besieged' - which is exactly LO-4; the opening inference about the gathering is LO-2.
The advocate-to-outlaw transformation is character change driven by Mandela's cause, LO-2, not a fact to be looked up.
'I was born free' has to be matched to the sense Mandela gives it (the illusory freedom of boyhood). Expression-to-meaning, LO-4, rather than a plain retrieval.
Describes what happened on 10 May as narrated; information extraction, LO-1.
Mandela's view of oppressor and oppressed is his message about freedom, LO-2.
What the oath-day speech covered is set out in the text; retrieval of its content, LO-1.
The text itself names the colours of the new flag in the jets' smoke trail, so the answer is extracted rather than interpreted; LO-1, not the figurative-language outcome.
Mandela's assessment of apartheid's deep and lasting wound is his judgement on his country's history - LO-2 rather than a single retrievable fact.
A 120-word presentation draft comparing Valli's desire with Mandela's vision, with a set opening line. Composition in a given format and register, C-E1.2.
Another 120-word presentation draft, this time comparing two childhoods. The marked skill is structured writing, so C-E1.2, not a literature outcome.
Choose a character from First Flight who met prejudice and trace its consequences for them - character-in-context analysis, LO-2, rather than a writing-format task.
Unpacks the two set phrases 'extraordinary human disaster' and 'glorious human achievement' - the expression-matching outcome, LO-4.
A full character sketch of Mandela. LO-2 names character analysis; LO-3 would apply if the question demanded quoted evidence.
Naming the twin obligations is retrieval (LO-1); the alternative wording adds why apartheid stopped him honouring them, which is context and message (LO-2).
The ideals he sets for South Africa's future are his vision - the writer's message, LO-2, consistent with the other 'future of South Africa' items.

Asks for the significance of freedom as the lesson presents it, i.e. the chapter's central theme, which LO-1 explicitly names. Not C-E1.2: the comment is to be drawn from the text, not from personal opinion.
A 120-word speech draft with prescribed opening and closing lines. Format, tone and structure are what is marked - C-E1.2.
First explain what 'behind bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness' means (LO-4), then support it with real-world examples of one's own (C-E1.2).
Write a dated diary entry expressing personal feeling. Diary format and first-person tone put this squarely in C-E1.2.
Part i asks what 'overwhelmed with a sense of history' conveys (LO-4); the MCQ part retrieves what the old system was replaced by (LO-1).
The lead MCQ judges the young Mandela's attitude as naive (LO-2); the follow-up asks what 'transitory freedoms' meant to him, an expression matched to its sense (LO-4).

The lead part asks the learner to identify the extract's form as an autobiographical account - a question about genre, which only the C-E1.4 competency covers; the later parts retrieve what the day cost (LO-1).
Mandela's opinion of his people as the country's real wealth is his message (LO-2); the part on comparing them to the purest diamonds is his figurative language (LO-6).
Infer what Mandela was like as father and as leader - character inference across the whole text, LO-2.
Having been given Mandela's definition, the learner must offer their own. That is expression of an opinion with reasoning, C-E1.2, not analysis of the text.
'Justify his statement' asks the learner to build the argument themselves; C-E1.2 names reasoning and justifying. LO-2 would cover merely reporting what Mandela believed.
Bare 'what are they' version of the twin-obligations question - retrieval only, so LO-1 without the LO-2 half.
Describes the events of 10 May 1994 on the streets of Pretoria. Narrative detail, LO-1.
Lists the boyhood freedoms named in the text (running in the fields, swimming, roasting mealies). Retrieval, LO-1; the version that asks for the contrast with basic freedom is the LO-2 item.
What pained him - being unable to thank the patriots who died - is his inner state, LO-2.
The route to the presidency (the election, 252 of 400 seats) is narrated fact; retrieval, LO-1.
Why he joined the ANC turns on his realisation that everyone's freedom was curtailed - motive, LO-2.
A list of the hardships the text records. Information extraction, LO-1, not an analysis of what they cost him.
Mandela's claim that people, not minerals, are a nation's wealth is a value judgement - the writer's message, LO-2, matching the MCQ version of the same item.
